name: Hair transplant stereo-microscope

card.summary: A binocular microscope used by hair-transplant technicians to dissect donor tissue into follicular units, protecting the follicles that become the new hairline.
card.note: Clinic equipment rather than a consumer product.

quick.overview:
In strip-harvest hair transplantation (FUT), the donor strip of scalp is cut into small grafts under a stereo-microscope. The magnification lets technicians trim excess fibrous and fatty tissue while keeping the hair follicles intact, so that more grafts survive to grow as natural-looking hair.

Wikipedia credits B.L. Limmer with introducing the stereo-microscope for this purpose in the late 1980s. Patients do not use the device; it is part of how a clinic prepares grafts for a fuller-looking hairline.
quick.how: Technicians work under magnification to separate follicular units, the natural one-to-four-hair groups, before they are placed in the recipient area. In follicular unit extraction (FUE), units are taken individually with small punches rather than from a strip.
quick.risks: The microscope itself carries no risk to patients. Outcomes depend on the surgery and the team; FUT leaves a linear scar and about two weeks of recovery, while FUE leaves small punctate scars and under a week of recovery, per Wikipedia.

lead: A stereo-microscope is a binocular microscope used in hair transplantation to dissect donor tissue into follicular units. It lets technicians trim excess tissue from a harvested strip while protecting the follicles.[1]

For appearance, careful dissection helps preserve grafts so a transplanted hairline looks natural and fills in. Wikipedia credits B.L. Limmer with introducing the stereo-microscope for this work in the late 1980s.[1]
Dissection under a microscope is part of strip harvesting (FUT). In follicular unit extraction (FUE), which uses 0.6-1.0 mm punches, grafts are harvested individually.[1]

chain: Follicular units separated with follicles protected
More intact grafts transplanted for a fuller hairline
angle.text: Patients benefit through the quality of the grafts their surgeon places. Microscopic dissection is how many clinics prepare strip grafts so as to keep follicles undamaged.

infobox: Late 1980s (per Wikipedia, credited to B.L. Limmer)

paras: In strip harvesting, workers use binocular stereo-microscopes to trim fibrous and fatty tissue from the donor strip while protecting follicles.[1]

FUT removes a scalp strip, leaving a linear scar that hair usually covers, with about two weeks of recovery. FUE extracts individual units with 0.6-1.0 mm punches, leaves punctate scars, needs under a week of recovery, takes longer and costs more.[1]

timeline.event: B.L. Limmer is credited with introducing the stereo-microscope for graft dissection.[1]
